title: Ludi. Certamen navium (finis)
titleEn: The Boat Race Won — Aeneid V.201–285
about: The race for the ships comes to its end. Sergestus, cutting the turn too close, runs the Centaur onto the rock and breaks his oars; his crew pole the ship free as best they can while Mnestheus, cheered by the accident, takes the Pristis out to open water, as swift as a dove startled from its cave. Mnestheus passes the stranded Sergestus, then Gyas, whose ship has lost her helmsman, and is left with Cloanthus alone before him. The crowds roar, and the two crews are spurred on, one by fear of losing what they have, the other by the confidence success brings, and the race would have been a dead heat if Cloanthus had not stretched his hands out to the sea and vowed a white bull, wine and entrails to the gods of the deep. The Nereids, Phorcus' company and Portunus himself hear him, and Portunus pushes the ship home. Aeneas proclaims Cloanthus the winner and distributes the prizes: three bullocks, wine and a talent of silver to each ship, a cloak embroidered with Ganymede's abduction for the victor, a coat of mail for Mnestheus, cauldrons and silver bowls for Gyas. Last of all Sergestus limps into harbour like a half-crushed snake, and Aeneas, glad that ship and crew are saved, gives him a Cretan slave-woman and her twin sons. The scene reworks the chariot race of Iliad XXIII, with sea-gods taking the place of Homer's helping Athena.

sentences.t: Attulit ipse viris optatum casus honorem.
sentences.l: Brought, itself, to the men the longed-for honour, chance.
sentences.i: Chance itself brought the men the honour they had longed for.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Ipse' agrees with 'casus' ('chance itself'): the race is decided by an accident, not by skill. 'Viris' is a dative of the person for whom, here Mnestheus and his crew, who are named only in the next lines. 'Optatum' is the perfect passive participle of 'opto', 'wished for'. Now and again a Virgilian sentence announces what is to happen before explaining it; the next sentence gives the explanation ('namque').

sentences.t:
Namque furens animi dum proram ad saxa suburguet
interior, spatioque subit Sergestus iniquo,
infelix saxis in procurrentibus haesit.
sentences.l:
For raging in mind, while he presses his prow toward the rocks
on the inside, and enters a space too narrow, Sergestus,
unlucky, on jutting rocks he stuck fast.
sentences.i: For Sergestus, wild with eagerness, was pressing his prow in toward the rocks on the inside track, and had driven into too narrow a gap; unlucky man, he stuck fast on the jutting reefs.
sentences.n: 'Furens animi' is 'raging in mind': 'animi' has the form of a genitive but is a locative, 'in mind' (as in 'aeger animi', 'pendere animi'); grammars often class it as a genitive of respect. 'Dum' with a present indicative ('suburguet', Greenough's spelling of 'suburget', from 'suburgeo', 'press close up to') marks an action in progress when the main verb 'haesit' (perfect of 'haereo', 'stuck') falls; 'subit', 'goes in under', is the second verb of the 'dum' clause. 'Interior' is a comparative, 'on the inner track'; 'spatio… iniquo' is an ablative of attendant circumstance, a gap that was uneven or too narrow ('iniquus', 'unfavourable'). 'Infelix' agrees with Sergestus. Sergestus was the captain of the Centaur.

sentences.t:
Concussae cautes, et acuto in murice remi
obnixi crepuere, inlisaque prora pependit.
sentences.l:
Shaken the crags were, and on the sharp murex-rock the oars
braced against it cracked, and the dashed-on prow hung fast.
sentences.i: The rocks shook; the oars, braced against the sharp spike of stone, snapped, and the smashed prow was left hanging there.
sentences.n: 'Concussae' is a perfect passive participle with 'cautes' ('sunt' understood; 'concutio', 'shake'). 'Murice' is the ablative of 'murex', a spiny sea-shell and so a sharp point of rock. 'Obnixi', from the deponent 'obnitor', 'strain against', is a perfect participle with active sense; 'crepuere' is 'crepuerunt', 'cracked' (the -ere ending for -erunt, as flagged in Book I). 'Inlisa' is the participle of 'inlido', 'dash against'; 'pependit' the perfect of 'pendeo', 'hung', the ship being caught fast with her bows on the rock.

sentences.t:
Consurgunt nautae et magno clamore morantur,
ferratasque trudes et acuta cuspide contos
expediunt, fractosque legunt in gurgite remos.
sentences.l:
Rise up the sailors and with a great shout delay,
and iron-shod poles and with sharp point boathooks
they make ready, and the broken oars gather in the eddy.
sentences.i: The crew leap up with loud shouting and lose time there; they bring out iron-tipped poles and sharp-pointed boat-hooks, and fish their broken oars out of the swirling water.
sentences.n: 'Morantur' is used absolutely, 'they are delayed, they lose time' (the race goes on without them). 'Trudes' are pushing-poles and 'contos' boat-poles (Greek 'kontos'); 'ferratas' is 'iron-shod', and 'acuta cuspide' an ablative of quality, 'with a sharp point', with 'contos'. 'Expediunt' is 'get ready' (literally 'free the feet'); 'legunt' is 'pick up', as with something scattered. The 'que… et' pair joins the two kinds of pole. 'Gurgite' is the whirlpool of churned water round the stranded ship.

sentences.t:
At laetus Mnestheus successuque acrior ipso
agmine remorum celeri ventisque vocatis
prona petit maria et pelago decurrit aperto.
sentences.l:
But glad Mnestheus, and by success itself keener,
with a swift column of oars and winds called on,
sloping seas seeks and runs down on the open sea.
sentences.i: But Mnestheus, glad, and made keener by the very success, calls on the winds, and with a rapid drive of oars makes for the sloping water and runs down it into the open sea.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Successu… ipso' is an ablative of cause with the comparative 'acrior', 'keener because of the success itself' (his rival's disaster has given him hope). 'Agmine remorum celeri' is an ablative of manner: 'agmen' is a column in march, here the close-ordered stroke of the oars. 'Ventis vocatis' is an ablative absolute: he invokes the winds, in the epic way. 'Prona maria' are the seas sloping away ahead of the ship, down which she 'runs' ('decurrit'); 'pelago aperto' is an ablative of the way, 'over the open sea'.

sentences.t:
Qualis spelunca subito commota columba,
cui domus et dulces latebroso in pumice nidi,
fertur in ana volans, plausumque exterrita pennis
dat tecto ingentem, mox aere lapsa quieto
radit iter liquidum, celeres neque commovet alas:
sentences.l:
As a dove, from a cave suddenly roused,
for whom is home and sweet nests in the hollowed pumice,
is borne flying into the fields, and a clapping, terrified, with wings
gives to the roof huge, soon in the quiet air gliding
skims her liquid path, and her swift wings does not stir:
sentences.i: As a dove suddenly startled from her cave, whose home and sweet nests are in its hollowed rock, flies out over the fields, and in her fright sets the roof ringing with a great clatter of wings, then, gliding in the still air, skims her clear path, her swift wings unmoving:
sentences.n: The print has "ana", a misprint for "arva", corrected here: 'in arva', 'into the fields'. The Latin Library prints 'arua'. A simile: 'qualis… columba' is answered by 'sic' in the next unit. 'Spelunca' is an ablative of source with 'commota' ('stirred from the cave'); 'cui domus… nidi' is a dative of possession ('sunt mihi' again). 'Pumice' is porous rock, 'latebroso' 'full of hiding-places'. 'Exterrita' is a perfect participle of 'exterreo'; 'plausum… dat… tecto' is 'gives a clap to the roof', the cave echoing with her wing-beats. 'Aere lapsa' is 'gliding in the air' (the ablative of route, from deponent 'labor'); 'aere' is the Greek 'aer', three syllables, a-e-re. 'Liquidum' is 'clear, fluid'. Compare the dove of Iliad XXI.493 ff., which darts into a hollow rock; here the bird shows the speed of a ship.

sentences.t:
sic Mnestheus, sic ipsa fuga secat ultima Pristis
aequora, sic illam fert impetus ipse volantem.
sentences.l:
so Mnestheus, so herself in flight cuts, the last, Pristis
the waters, so her the very impetus carries as she flies.
sentences.i: So Mnestheus, so the Pristis herself, till now last, cuts the water in her flight, and so the very momentum bears her flying onward.
sentences.n: The 'sic… sic… sic' answers the simile's 'qualis'; the threefold 'sic' drives the comparison home. 'Mnestheus' stands for his ship by metonymy, and the Pristis is named in apposition. 'Ipsa' (short -a, so nominative: the metre decides) goes with 'Pristis', 'the Pristis herself'; 'fuga' is an ablative (long -a), 'in her flight'; 'ultima' is 'last' up to now. 'Illam… volantem' is a participle agreeing with 'illam', 'her, as she flies'; 'impetus ipse' is the very momentum that now carries her on.

sentences.t:
Et primum in scopulo luctantem deserit alto
Sergestum, brevibusque vadis frustraque vocantem
auxilia, et fractis discentem currere remis.
sentences.l:
And first on the rock struggling he leaves lofty
Sergestus, and in shallow shoals and vainly calling
for help, and with broken oars learning to run.
sentences.i: First he leaves Sergestus behind, struggling on his towering rock in the shallows, calling in vain for help and learning to run with broken oars.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Luctantem… vocantem… discentem' are three present participles agreeing with 'Sergestum' (placed in the next line). 'Alto' with 'scopulo' is 'high'; 'brevibus vadis' (ablative of place) 'in the shoals', from 'brevia', 'shallows'. 'Discentem currere' is 'learning to run', an ironic way of saying that the broken-oared ship has to learn a new way of moving: 'currere' is a complementary infinitive.

sentences.t:
Inde Gyan ipsamque ingenti mole Chimaeram
consequitur;
sentences.l:
Then Gyas and the Chimaera herself, of huge bulk,
he overtakes;
sentences.i: Next he overtakes Gyas and the huge Chimaera herself;
sentences.n: 'Gyan' is the accusative singular of the Greek name Gyas, with the Greek ending -an. 'Ipsam' marks the ship as well as her captain. 'Ingenti mole' is an ablative of quality, 'of huge bulk': the Chimaera is the biggest ship in the race. 'Consequitur' is the present of the deponent 'consequor', 'overtake'.

sentences.t: cedit, quoniam spoliata magistro est.
sentences.l: she yields, since robbed of her helmsman she is.
sentences.i: she gives way, because she has lost her helmsman.
sentences.n: 'Cedit' is the present, 'gives way, falls back'; its subject is the Chimaera. 'Spoliata… est' is a perfect passive of 'spolio', 'strip'; 'magistro' is an ablative of separation, 'of her master', i.e. the helmsman Menoetes whom Gyas threw overboard in the previous part.

sentences.t: Solus iamque ipso superest in fine Cloanthus:
sentences.l: Alone and now at the very finish remains Cloanthus:
sentences.i: Now only Cloanthus is left, close to the very finish:
sentences.n: 'Solus' is predicative, 'alone'. 'Ipso in fine' is 'at the very end (of the course)', at the point where the finishing line is near. The colon leads from the situation to the one man whom Mnestheus now chases.

sentences.t: quem petit, et summis adnixus viribus urguet.
sentences.l: whom he makes for, and, leaning on with utmost strength, presses.
sentences.i: Mnestheus goes after him, and straining with all his strength bears down hard.
sentences.n: 'Quem' is a connecting relative, 'him'. 'Adnixus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'adnitor', 'straining' (active sense), with 'summis viribus', an ablative of manner. 'Urguet' is Greenough's spelling of 'urget', 'presses hard'. 'Summis' is 'the topmost, the utmost'.

sentences.t:
Tum vero ingeminat clamor, cunctique sequentem
instigant studiis, resonatque fragoribus aether.
sentences.l:
Then indeed redoubles the shout, and all him following
urge on with cheers, and resounds with crashes the sky.
sentences.i: Then indeed the shouting redoubles, and all of them urge the pursuer on with their cheers, and the sky rings with the din.
sentences.n: 'Tum vero' is 'then indeed', and marks the turn to the final burst. 'Ingeminat' is intransitive, 'redoubles'. 'Sequentem' is a present participle, 'the one who follows', i.e. Mnestheus; 'studiis' is an ablative of means, 'with partisan cheering'. 'Aether', Greek for the bright upper air, is the nominative singular here. In Iliad XXIII the Greek spectators also shout on their favourites.

sentences.t:
Hi proprium decus et partum indignantur honorem
ni teneant, vitamque volunt pro laude pacisci;
sentences.l:
These their own glory and gained honour are indignant
if they should not hold, and life they are willing for praise to barter;
sentences.i: One side is furious at the thought of losing the glory that is theirs and the honour already won, and is ready to barter life for praise;
sentences.n: 'Hi' are the crew of Cloanthus, 'hos' in the next unit those of Mnestheus. 'Indignantur ni teneant' is 'they are angry (at the thought) that they might not keep it': 'ni' is 'nisi', 'unless', and the subjunctive 'teneant' makes the possible loss a case supposed inside their feeling, so that 'ni teneant' is 'if they should fail to keep it'. 'Proprium decus' is 'their own distinction'; 'partum' is the perfect participle of 'pario', 'won'. 'Pacisci' is the deponent infinitive, 'to bargain, make a deal'.

sentences.t: hos successus alit:
sentences.l: these success feeds:
sentences.i: The other side is fed by its success:
sentences.n: 'Hos' is the other crew; 'alit' is 'feeds, nourishes'. The colon leads to the reason.

sentences.t: possunt, quia posse videntur.
sentences.l: they can, because to be able they seem.
sentences.i: strength is theirs because they seem to have it.
sentences.n: 'Posse videntur' has the passive 'videntur' as a personal verb with the infinitive: 'they are seen to be able', 'they seem to be able'. The line has become a saying.

sentences.t:
Et fors aequatis cepissent praemia rostris,
ni palmas ponto tendens utrasque Cloanthus
fudissetque preces, divosque in vota vocasset:
sentences.l:
And perhaps, with the prows made level, they would have taken the prizes,
unless his palms to the sea stretching both Cloanthus
had poured out prayers, and the gods into vows had called:
sentences.i: And perhaps, with the prows level, the prize would have been theirs, had Cloanthus not stretched both hands out toward the sea, poured out prayers, and called the gods to hear his vows:
sentences.n: 'Fors' is an old noun used adverbially, 'perhaps'. A past unreal condition: 'cepissent' (pluperfect subjunctive of 'capio') is answered by 'ni… fudisset… vocasset' ('ni' is 'nisi'); 'vocasset' is the syncopated 'vocavisset'. 'Aequatis rostris' is an ablative absolute; 'ponto' is a dative of direction, 'to the sea'; 'palmas… utrasque' is 'both palms', held up in prayer. 'In vota vocasset' is 'summoned them to his vows'. Where Homer's gods interfere in the chariot race of Iliad XXIII (Apollo and Athena), Virgil brings in the gods of the sea.

sentences.t:
“Di, quibus imperium est pelagi, quorum aequora curro,
vobis laetus ego hoc candentem in litore taurum
constituam ante aras, voti reus, extaque salsos
porriciam in fluctus et vina liquentia fundam.”
sentences.l:
“Gods, to whom the empire of the sea belongs, whose waters I run,
to you, glad, I this shining bull on the shore
will set before the altars, a debtor of the vow, and the entrails into the salt
waves will cast and wine flowing will pour.”
sentences.i: “Gods, whose is the sovereignty of the sea and whose waters I travel, I will gladly set this gleaming white bull on the shore before your altars, owing you the vow I make; I will cast its entrails into the salt waves and pour out clear wine.”
sentences.n: The marks “ ” enclose Cloanthus's prayer, a vow: if the gods help him he will sacrifice. 'Quibus imperium est' is a dative of possession; 'aequora curro' has 'curro' ('run over') governing the accusative of the sea. 'Voti reus' is 'liable on a vow', one who has made a vow and is bound to pay it. 'Constituam', 'porriciam' and 'fundam' are futures; 'porricio' is the ritual word for offering entrails, where the Latin Library prints 'proiciam', 'I will throw'. 'Candentem' is 'gleaming white'; 'extaque… in fluctus' is the offering of the entrails to the waves. 'Liquentia' is a present participle, 'flowing, clear'.

sentences.t:
Dixit, eumque imis sub fluctibus audiit omnis
Nereidum Phorcique chorus Panopeaque virgo,
et pater ipse manu magna Portunus euntem
impulit;
sentences.l:
He spoke, and him beneath the deepest waves heard the whole
chorus of Nereids and of Phorcus, and Panopea the maiden,
and the father himself, with a great hand, Portunus, her going
pushed;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the whole company of the Nereids and of Phorcus, with the maiden Panopea, heard him from deep beneath the waves, and father Portunus himself, with his great hand, pushed the ship forward as she went;
sentences.n: 'Dixit' is the usual brief close of a speech. 'Omnis' is the nominative singular, agreeing with 'chorus'. 'Nereidum' is the genitive plural of the Greek 'Nereis', 'Nereid' (the sea-nymphs, daughters of Nereus), in the ordinary -um of consonant stems. 'Phorci' is the genitive of the sea-god Phorcus (Phorcys), here with his own retinue: 'the company of Nereids and of Phorcus'; Panopea is a Nereid. 'Portunus' is the Roman god of harbours, called 'pater', 'father'; 'euntem' is an accusative participle, 'as she went' (the object is the ship, understood). 'Imis sub fluctibus' is 'beneath the lowest waves'; the sea-gods are the answer to the prayer. The line is hard to fit: 'Nereidum' has four syllables, and the last syllable of 'chorus' is lengthened at the caesura.

sentences.t:
illa Noto citius volucrique sagitta
ad terram fugit, et portu se condidit alto.
sentences.l:
she, than the South wind quicker and than a winged arrow,
toward land flees, and in harbour hid herself deep.
sentences.i: She, swifter than the south wind or a flying arrow, sped to land and hid herself in the deep harbour.
sentences.n: 'Illa' is the ship (the Scylla), and the comparison is made with the ablatives 'Noto' and 'volucri sagitta' after the comparative 'citius', an adverb. 'Fugit' is a historic present (the short u shows it is not the perfect), and 'se condidit' ('hid herself') continues it in the perfect. 'Portu… alto' is an ablative of place, 'in the deep harbour'. Wind and arrow are the standard Virgilian measures of speed; the 'arrow' is 'volucris', 'winged'.

sentences.t:
Tum satus Anchisa, cunctis ex more vocatis,
victorem magna praeconis voce Cloanthum
declarat viridique advelat tempora lauro,
muneraque in naves ternos optare iuvencos,
vinaque et argenti magnum dat ferre talentum.
sentences.l:
Then the one sprung from Anchises, all by custom having been summoned,
victor with a great herald's voice Cloanthus
declares, and with green laurel veils his brow,
and gifts for the ships three bulls apiece to choose,
and wines and of silver a great talent gives to carry off.
sentences.i: Then Anchises' son, having called all together as custom required, proclaims Cloanthus the victor in the herald's great voice, binds green laurel about his brow, and gives gifts for the ships: three bullocks apiece to choose, with wine and a great talent of silver to carry away.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Satus Anchisa' is 'sprung from Anchises', the perfect participle of 'sero' with an ablative of origin; 'Anchisa' is the Latinised ablative of the Greek name, and the periphrasis stands for Aeneas. 'Cunctis ex more vocatis' is an ablative absolute, 'all summoned according to custom'. 'Praeconis' is the herald, as in Homer's games. 'Advelat' is 'veils, wreathes'. 'In naves' means 'for the ships'; 'ternos' is distributive, 'three each'; 'optare' and 'ferre' are infinitives of purpose after 'dat', 'gives (them) to choose / to carry'. 'Talentum', neuter, is the Greek unit of weight.

sentences.t: Ipsis praecipuos ductoribus addit honores:
sentences.l: To the captains themselves special honours he adds:
sentences.i: To the captains themselves he adds special honours:
sentences.n: 'Ipsis… ductoribus' is a dative, 'to the captains themselves', as against the crews who have already been rewarded. 'Praecipuos' is 'particular, special'. The colon leads to the list of gifts.

sentences.t:
victori chlamydem auratam, quam plurima circum
purpura maeandro duplici Meliboea cucurrit,
intextusque puer frondosa regius Ida
veloces iaculo cervos cursuque fatigat,
sentences.l:
to the victor a cloak gold-embroidered, around which very much
purple in a double meander, Meliboean, ran,
and woven in, a boy, a royal one, on leafy Ida
swift deer with javelin and with running wears out,
sentences.i: to the victor a gold-embroidered cloak, edged all round by a wide band of Meliboean purple in a double meander, and woven into it a royal boy on leafy Ida tires out the swift deer with javelin and with running,
sentences.n: 'Chlamydem' is the accusative singular of the Greek-derived noun 'chlamys', a short cloak, with a Latin -em ending. 'Auratam' is 'gold-worked'; in 'quam… circum… cucurrit' the preposition 'circum' follows its relative, 'around which'. 'Plurima purpura', 'a great deal of purple', 'Meliboea' ('from Meliboea', a Thessalian town known for purple dye), is the subject, and 'maeandro duplici' an ablative of manner, a double wave-pattern like the winding river Maeander. 'Intextus' is a perfect participle, 'woven in'. 'Frondosa Ida' is an ablative of place; the boy is Ganymede, unnamed, a prince of Troy, 'regius'. 'Iaculo' and 'cursu' are ablatives of means, 'fatigat' 'wears out' the game he hunts. The ekphrasis, the pause to describe a work of art, runs to 257.

sentences.t:
acer, anhelanti similis, quem praepes ab Ida
sublimem pedibus rapuit Iovis armiger uncis;
sentences.l:
keen, like to one panting, whom the swift-winged from Ida
aloft snatched up with feet, Jove's armour-bearer, hooked;
sentences.i: eager, and like one out of breath, whom Jove's swift-winged armour-bearer swept up from Ida and carried off aloft in its hooked talons;
sentences.n: 'Acer' is 'keen'; 'anhelanti similis' has the dative with 'similis', 'like one panting'. 'Praepes', 'swift of wing', is an adjective with 'armiger'; 'Iovis armiger', 'Jove's armour-bearer', is the eagle that carries the god's thunderbolt, and the story is the rape of Ganymede. 'Sublimem' is a predicative accusative, 'lifted on high', and 'pedibus… uncis' an ablative of means, 'with hooked feet'. 'Ab Ida' is 'from Ida'.

sentences.t:
longaevi palmas nequiquam ad sidera tendunt
custodes, saevitque canum latratus in auras.
sentences.l:
aged, their palms in vain toward the stars stretch
his guards, and rages the barking of dogs into the air.
sentences.i: his aged guardians stretch their hands up to the stars in vain, and the baying of the hounds rages upward into the air.
sentences.n: 'Longaevi… custodes' are 'the aged attendants' left behind on Ida. 'Palmas… tendunt' ('stretch their hands') is the gesture of prayer or despair. 'Canum' is the genitive plural of 'canis', 'of dogs'; 'latratus' is the nominative of the fourth declension, 'barking'. 'Saevit', 'rages', is used of sound; 'in auras' is 'into the breezes', i.e. up into the air.

sentences.t:
At qui deinde locum tenuit virtute secundum,
levibus huic hamis consertam auroque trilicem
loricam, quam Demoleo detraxerat ipse
victor apud rapidum Simoënta sub Ilio alto,
donat habere viro, decus et tutamen in armis.
sentences.l:
But to him who next the place held in prowess second,
with smooth hooks linked and with gold triple-threaded
a corselet, which from Demoleos had stripped himself
as victor by the rapid Simois under lofty Ilium,
he gives to have, an ornament and a protection in arms.
sentences.i: To the man who next held second place for prowess he gives a corselet to keep, its smooth rings interlinked and triple-threaded with gold, which he himself, as victor, had stripped from Demoleos beside the swift Simois under lofty Ilium, an ornament and a safeguard in battle.
sentences.n: The sentence starts with 'qui… tenuit', 'who held', whose antecedent is 'huic', 'to him'; 'secundum' is 'second' with 'locum'. 'Consertam' (perfect participle of 'consero', 'join together') and 'trilicem' ('three-threaded', 'trilix') both agree with 'loricam': a mail-coat of 'hooks', i.e. interlinked rings, worked with gold. 'Demoleo' is a dative of separation after 'detraxerat' ('had stripped from'); 'Simoënta' is the accusative singular of the Greek river-name Simois with the Greek -a ending (the 'ë' marks the diaeresis). 'Donat habere' is 'gives to have', an infinitive of purpose; 'decus et tutamen' are in apposition, 'tutamen' being 'protection', from 'tueor'.

sentences.t:
Vix illam famuli Phegeus Sagarisque ferebant
multiplicem, conixi umeris;
sentences.l:
Scarcely it the servants Phegeus and Sagaris were carrying,
many-folded, straining with shoulders;
sentences.i: Two servants, Phegeus and Sagaris, could hardly carry it, many-layered as it was, straining under it with their shoulders;
sentences.n: 'Vix' goes with 'ferebant', the imperfect of effort, 'were carrying (with difficulty)'. 'Famuli' is a noun in the nominative plural, 'servants', with the two Greek names in apposition. 'Multiplicem' agrees with 'illam' (the mail-coat) and means 'many-layered, heavy'; 'conixi' is the perfect participle of 'conitor', 'straining', 'umeris' an ablative of means. The semicolon sets the weight of the mail now against its former wearer. 'Phegeus' has the Greek ending -eus, one syllable (Phe-geus).

sentences.t:
indutus at olim
Demoleos cursu palantes Troas agebat.
sentences.l:
clothed in it, yet, once
Demoleos on the run the straying Trojans was driving.
sentences.i: yet once, wearing it, Demoleos was chasing scattered Trojans at the run.
sentences.n: 'Indutus' is a perfect participle of 'induo', 'put on', in the middle sense, 'clothed in it'; 'at' is contrastive, 'but' (heavy now for two, light once for one). 'Demoleos' is the Greek nominative; 'palantes', 'wandering, scattered', is the present participle of the deponent 'palor' (the Latin Library prints the accusative plural 'palantis', the same form in a different spelling); 'Troas' is the Greek accusative plural of the Trojan name, 'Trojans'. 'Cursu' is an ablative of manner, 'at a run'; 'agebat' is 'was driving', as of a herd. The line scans only with a long first syllable in 'palantes' and a short -as in 'Troas' before the vowel of 'agebat'.

sentences.t:
Tertia dona facit geminos ex aere lebetas,
cymbiaque argento perfecta atque aspera signis.
sentences.l:
Third gifts he makes, twin from bronze cauldrons,
and bowls with silver finished and rough with figures.
sentences.i: As the third prize he gives a pair of bronze cauldrons, and cups of finished silver, bristling with embossed figures.
sentences.n: 'Tertia dona facit' is 'makes (them) third gifts', i.e. as the third prize. 'Lebetas' is the Greek accusative plural of 'lebes', 'cauldron', as often in prize-lists; the third prize of the chariot race in Iliad XXIII is also a cauldron. 'Cymbia', 'little bowls, cups', is another Greek loan-word; 'argento perfecta' is an ablative of material, 'finished in silver', and 'aspera signis' 'rough with figures', raised work in relief ('signis' is an ablative of respect or cause).

sentences.t:
Iamque adeo donati omnes opibusque superbi
puniceis ibant evincti tempora taenis,
sentences.l:
And now indeed, rewarded, all, and in riches proud,
with scarlet were going, bound as to the temples, ribbons,
sentences.i: And now all of them, rewarded and proud of their wealth, were walking away with their brows bound in scarlet ribbons,
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Iamque adeo', 'and by now indeed', marks the moment before the next event. 'Donati', 'having been given gifts', is a perfect participle from 'dono', which takes the person as object and the gift in the ablative, so the passive makes the person the subject. 'Opibus… superbi' is an ablative of cause, 'proud of their wealth'. 'Evincti tempora' has an accusative of respect, 'bound as to their brows', with 'taenis' an ablative of means (a 'taenia' is a ribbon or fillet). The sentence is not finished: it is the first half of a 'cum inversum'.

sentences.t:
cum saevo e scopulo multa vix arte revolsus,
amissis remis atque ordine debilis uno,
inrisam sine honore ratem Sergestus agebat.
sentences.l:
when from the cruel rock with much art scarcely drawn free,
his oars lost and by one bank crippled,
a mocked, without honour, ship Sergestus was driving.
sentences.i: when Sergestus, wrenched free from the cruel rock with great skill and barely, his oars lost and one bank of them useless, was steering his jeered-at ship, with no prize to show.
sentences.n: 'Cum' with the indicative ('agebat') is the 'cum inversum': the real event comes in the 'when' clause, after the quiet scene in the main clause ('ibant'). 'Revolsus' is Greenough's spelling of 'revulsus', the perfect participle of 'revello', 'torn back, wrenched free'. 'Multa… arte' is 'with great skill' and 'vix' goes with it. 'Amissis remis' is an ablative absolute, 'ordine… uno' an ablative of respect, 'crippled in one bank' of oars. 'Inrisam', 'laughed at', is from 'inrideo'; 'sine honore' is 'without distinction', 'agebat' is 'was driving'.

sentences.i: Just as often a snake, caught on the crown of a road, which a bronze-tyred wheel has crossed slantwise, or a traveller has left half-dead and mangled with a heavy blow of a stone;
sentences.n: A simile, answered by 'tali' in 280. 'Qualis' introduces it: 'deprensus' is a participle, 'caught', with 'in aggere', 'on the raised roadbed'. 'Aerea' means 'of bronze'; 'quem' is object of both verbs. 'Obliquum' is an accusative adjective used as an adverb, 'slantwise'. 'Transiit' is the perfect of 'transeo', 'went across', here with an accusative. 'Gravis ictu' has 'ictu' as an ablative of respect, 'heavy in the stroke', and 'saxo' an ablative of means. 'Seminecem' and 'lacerum' are predicative accusatives, 'half-dead and mangled'; 'liquit' is the perfect of 'linquo', 'left'.

sentences.t:
nequiquam longos fugiens dat corpore tortus,
parte ferox, ardensque oculis, et sibila colla
arduus attollens, pars volnere clauda retentat
nexantem nodis seque in sua membra plicantem:
sentences.l:
in vain, long fleeing, gives with his body twistings,
in part fierce and blazing with his eyes, and hissing necks
upright lifting, part by the wound lame holds back
the knotting with coils and itself into its own limbs folding:
sentences.i: in vain he flees, making long winding loops with his body, fierce in one part and blazing in the eyes, and lifts his hissing neck high; the other part, lamed by the wound, holds him back as he twists himself in knots and folds himself into his own coils:
sentences.n: The subject, the snake, is the 'serpens' of 273. 'Tortus' is an accusative plural (fourth declension), 'twistings, coils'. 'Parte ferox' has an ablative of respect, 'fierce in one part'; 'ardens oculis' 'blazing with his eyes'. 'Sibila colla' are 'hissing necks', a poetic plural for the single neck, accusative object of 'attollens', 'lifting'; 'arduus' is 'upright'. 'Pars… clauda' is 'the other part, lame', 'volnere' being Greenough's spelling of 'vulnere'. 'Retentat' is the frequentative of 'retineo', 'holds back again and again'; 'nexantem' and 'plicantem' are accusative present participles with the understood object, 'him knotting himself in coils and folding himself into his own limbs'.

sentences.t: tali remigio navis se tarda movebat;
sentences.l: with such rowing the ship slow herself was moving;
sentences.i: With such rowing the slow ship dragged herself along;
sentences.n: 'Tali' answers 'qualis' of the simile. 'Remigio' is an ablative of means, 'by rowing' (the collective noun for the oars and oarsmen). 'Se movebat' is reflexive, 'moved herself', and 'tarda' is 'slow'.

sentences.t: vela facit tamen, et velis subit ostia plenis.
sentences.l: sails she makes nevertheless, and with sails full enters the harbour mouths.
sentences.i: Yet she makes sail, and with full sails enters the harbour mouth.
sentences.n: 'Vela facit' is the idiom 'makes sail, spreads sail'; 'tamen' sets the sails against the crippled oars. 'Velis… plenis' is an ablative of manner, 'with sails full' (with 'plenis' agreeing with 'velis'); 'subit ostia' is 'goes in at the mouth' of the harbour ('ostium' is a mouth or entrance).

sentences.t:
Sergestum Aeneas promisso munere donat,
servatam ob navem laetus sociosque reductos.
sentences.l:
Sergestus Aeneas with the promised gift rewards,
saved on account of the ship, glad, and the comrades brought back.
sentences.i: Aeneas rewards Sergestus with the gift he had promised, glad that the ship was saved and her crew brought back.
sentences.n: 'Donat' with an accusative of the person and an ablative of the gift ('promisso munere'), as with 'donati' above. 'Servatam… navem' and 'sociosque reductos' are accusatives after 'ob' with perfect participles, 'on account of the ship saved and the comrades brought back'; 'laetus' agrees with Aeneas. The promise is the one made to every competitor at the start.

sentences.t:
Olli serva datur, operum haud ignara Minervae,
Cressa genus, Pholoë, geminique sub ubere nati.
sentences.l:
To him a slave-woman is given, of works not ignorant of Minerva,
a Cretan by race, Pholoe, and twin beneath the breast sons.
sentences.i: To him is given a slave-woman skilled in the crafts of Minerva, Cretan by birth, Pholoe, with twin sons at her breast.
sentences.n: 'Olli' is the old dative of 'ille', 'to him' (an archaism Virgil likes); 'serva' is the woman slave. 'Operum… Minervae' is a genitive with 'ignara' ('not unfamiliar with'), the 'works of Minerva' being wool-working and other handiwork, over which that goddess presides. 'Cressa genus' has 'genus' as an accusative of respect, 'Cretan in race'. 'Pholoë' is the Greek name with the diaeresis on the 'e'. 'Nati' are in the nominative with the subject: the two sons come with her. In Iliad XXIII.263 the first prize is a woman skilled in handiwork; here she is the consolation prize.
